title: Twice the speed, how much more road?
hook: A car stops in 7 m from 30 km/h. Go twice as fast with the same brakes. How far now?

knows: faster cars take longer to stop
speeds in km/h and distances in metres
doesNotKnow: that braking distance grows with the square of speed

misconception: Double the speed, double the stopping distance.
objective: The learner can explain that with the same brakes, twice the speed needs four times the braking distance, because movement energy grows with the square of speed.

claims.text: With a steady braking deceleration a, the braking distance is v^2 / (2 a), so it grows with the square of speed.
claims.source: Constant-acceleration kinematics v^2 = v0^2 - 2 a d with final v = 0. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 2.

claims.text: At 5 m/s^2, braking from 30 km/h takes 6.9 m and from 60 km/h takes 27.8 m (four times as far); 90 km/h takes 62.5 m (nine times) and 120 km/h takes 111.1 m (sixteen times).
Movement (kinetic) energy is 1/2 m v^2, so twice the speed carries four times the energy.
claims.source: Definition of kinetic energy. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 7.

claims.text: The same brakes remove the same energy per metre: the braking force times distance equals the kinetic energy removed.
claims.source: Work-energy theorem: F d = 1/2 m v^2 with constant braking force F = m a. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 7.

claims.text: A deceleration of 5 m/s^2 is a typical hard-braking value on a dry road (about a friction coefficient of 0.5), not a universal one.
claims.source: a = mu g with mu about 0.5; typical dry-road braking decelerations are quoted around 5 to 8 m/s^2 (e.g. the UK Highway Code typical braking distances, 14 m from 30 mph and 75 m from 70 mph, imply about 6.4 m/s^2). Tagged as typical.

claims.text: The lesson shows braking distance only; reaction distance (speed times reaction time) adds more road on top and also grows with speed.
claims.source: Stated scope. Total stopping distance = v t_reaction + v^2 / (2 a) (UK Highway Code, rule 126, typical stopping distances).

recall.question: A cyclist brakes from 10 km/h in 1 m. With the same brakes, about how far does she need from 30 km/h?
recall.why: Braking distance grows with the square of speed: three times the speed needs nine times the distance.
